@@121126202 <h> What Republicans really mean when they blame ' DEI ' <p> In 1981 , Lee Atwater , the most influential Republican party strategist of the late 20th century , sat down for an off-the-record interview with the political scientist Alexander P Lamis . At the time , Atwater was a junior member of the Reagan administration , but he would later go on to run George HW Bush 's presidential campaign in 1988 and then become chair of the Republican National Committee in 1989 . <p> In perhaps the most revealing , and most infamous , portion of the interview , the hard-charging Republican operative explained to Lamis how Republican politicians could mask their racism -- and racist appeals to white voters -- behind a series of euphemisms . <p> You start out in 1954 by saying , ' N-word , N-word , N-word ' . By 1968 you ca n't say ' N-word ' -- that hurts you , backfires . So you say stuff like , uh , forced busing , states ' rights , and all that stuff , and you 're getting so abstract . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all these things you 're talking about are totally economic things and a byproduct of them is , blacks get hurt worse than whites ... ' We want to cut this , ' is much more abstract than even the busing thing , uh , and a hell of a lot more abstract than ' N-word , N-word ' . <p> Got that ? No need to utter the N-word out loud as there were plenty of other " abstract " ways to say it . <p> Today , more than four decades later , DEI has become the new N-word ; the new rightwing abstraction deployed by Republicans to conceal their anti-Black racism . DEI -- short for diversity , equity and inclusion -- is thrown around by high-profile conservatives , from the president of the United States downwards , for the express purpose of undermining Black people in public life . <p> Do n't believe me ? @@121145883 <p> Climate Transition Plans will become crucial for comms teams thanks to the EU 's directive on ESG , says Olly Lawder at Revolt . See these plans as an opportunity to align company values and let the world -- and your investors -- know about the great work you do . <p> The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive ( CSRD ) has raised the bar on Environment , Social , and Governance ( ESG ) reporting . It 's estimated that 50,000 companies with a presence in the EU will have to comply with the directive , which requires companies to share information on their monitoring of many ESG issues . The directive is purposefully technical , and this complexity can create a hurdle for communication and engagement . <p> But an opportunity does exist in the shape of the Climate Transition Plan ( CTP ) . The CTP is a mandatory part of the reporting and offers companies an opportunity to creatively communicate their roadmap to net zero . And while marketers may not be creating CTPs , they will certainly be communicating them . <p> The CTP translates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , granular , and powerful business strategy to show to stakeholders . As a mandatory part of CSRD , businesses should n't view the CTP as simply a compliance exercise but as an opportunity to stand out and deliver . <p> Knowing that businesses will be heavily focused on CTPs this year with CSRD coming into force , Revolt conducted quantitative research with over 400 marketing and PR leaders in the US who work at companies with offices in the EU . The aim was to find out just how much marketers know about the directive and whether they will embrace the creative opportunities that CTPs present in their marketing and communications . <h> Want to go deeper ? Ask The Drum <h> Making it happen <p> Reassuringly , we found that nearly 96% of marketeers are aware of CTPs . Given the importance and ramifications of CSRD , we were not surprised by this . However , 30% report that they are either unaware if their company has a CTP or that their company is not developing one . This is a worryingly high percentage , and clearly more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aware of their climate transition responsibilities . <p> The good news is that all respondents agree -- either strongly or somewhat -- that CTPs represent good comms opportunities . But when asked about the extent of communications planning around CTPs for the next 12 months , only a third of respondents said they have a specific plan for communicating transition plans . Additionally , 65% reported that CTP communication was not in the broader communications plan , and 71% said they had n't budgeted for CTP communications . <p> So , while there is a good understanding of the marketing opportunity with CTPs , there is a real gap in terms of actually making it happen . When we addressed this with respondents , we found a variety of reasons for the slow or lacking movement in communicating CTPs . <p> Concern about accidentally greenwashing is the number one barrier to creatively engaging on climate transition plans . This was followed by a perceived difficulty in engaging audiences in what some consider a ' depressing topic , ' as well as audiences lacking interest in the subject matter . Other @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ out of their comfort zone with the topic . <p> However , these barriers can and should be overcome . I believe that there are three things marketers and corporate affairs teams should keep in mind to ensure effective communication of transition plans . <p> Advertisement <h> Interested investors <p> Climate change is n't a future concern ; it 's already upon us -- and investors are looking to invest in businesses that build resilience to climate risks and are ready to take on climate opportunities . Almost 99% of leading global insurance companies have now set a low-carbon transition objective within their investment portfolios , according to Blackrock . <p> While CTPs existed before CSRD , they lacked granularity . The new directive will create a groundswell of information that investors will look at , including the disclosure of climate-related risks , transition-related opportunities , investment plans for low-carbon technologies , impacts on staff , scenario-planning , and financial allocation for activity . <p> The CTP is an opportunity to translate your net-zero strategy into a powerful investment story -- a story of resilience , adaptability , and competitive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forms part of an ongoing dialogue and is a way to update investors on your transition progress . <p> Advertisement <h> Engaging employees <p> Every stakeholder plays a role in delivering on your CTP , but none is as important as your employees . Employees are potential champions and crucial implementers of your transition strategies . Employees play a role across all three principles of the CTP -- Ambition , Action , and Accountability -- and they act as change agents who can ensure the CTP does not just live in a document . <p> Showcasing how individual roles directly contribute to broader goals creates a compelling narrative that will help retain talent who see sustainability as a personal mission rather than a corporate imperative . To transition successfully , businesses will need people with the right skill sets and CTP comms that hero employees -- and show that measurable impact can help to attract future talent who value sustainability . <h> Suggested newsletters for you <h> Daily Briefing <h> Daily <p> Catch up on the most important stories of the day , curated by our editorial team . <h> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a curated digest of the most important marketing stories and expert insights from our global team . <h> The Drum Insider <h> Once a month <p> Learn how to pitch to our editors and get published on The Drum . <h> Value added <p> For effective transition planning , businesses must engage their value chain because , in most cases , Scope 3 emissions ( all indirect emissions relating to business activity , excluding utilities ) represent the largest portion of a business 's carbon footprint . So , while CTPs are individual to each business , they can only be achieved with systemic change across suppliers and geographies . It 's important that CTPs deliver and communicate a detailed and quantifiable picture of the value chain , including its most opaque areas . <p> View the CTP not as a supplier compliance checklist but rather a communication device to highlight a shared purpose between your business and your value chain . " <p> And a Reddit user , Masofon , replied : " There is only a risk of a subsidence if you cut the tree down . <p> " Additionally , yes , the roots of the tree if only 6m/7m away from the house will likely be in the way of an extension and you could kill the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that serves to anchor the tree .. and then potential subsidence . <p> " The level of potential subsidence depends on the age/size of the tree . <p> " Please do n't cut down a mature oak tree .. just .. pick a house that does n't have any trees if that is what you 'd want to do . Tree has probably been there longer than the house and would be there hundreds of years after too . On that note , the tree may have a Tree Preservation Order on it anyway . " <p> According to the Woodland Trust , tree roots , such as those from oak trees , can cause subsidence - this is where your house becomes uneven , and cracks in walls , ceilings , doorways and even joists can form , due to severe damage to your home 's foundations . <h> Trending <p> Invalid email <p> We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you 've consented to and to improve our understanding of you . This may include adverts from us and 3rd parties based on our understanding . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Policy <p> The Woodland Trust explains : " When tree roots grow into clay soil and take up enough moisture , they cause the soil to dry out and shrink . This can cause building foundations on the clay to move , triggering the signs of subsidence . <p> " Luckily , modern buildings are n't as affected by subsidence caused by trees . Houses built before the 1950s are most at risk as their foundations are shallower , making them more susceptible to movement . Subsidence is also more likely during periods of wet followed by extreme dry weather -- something we can expect to see more of due to climate change . <p> " Certain types of trees may be more likely to cause subsidence than others . Trees which thrive on a smaller amount of water are less likely to do so , while trees requiring more water are more likely to dry out shrinkable clay soils . We are too poor to continue a policy of self-harm , says James Price <p> A friend came back from a trip to the United States recently and told me her biggest takeaway was how warm every home and business is there , even in the bitter cold of winter . Back in Blighty , this friend is always wrapped in more layers than an F Scott Fitzgerald metaphor . But in the US , no one worried about the electricity bill , or letting down money saving expert Martin Lewis by fiddling with the thermostat . <p> This simple observation speaks volumes about how our quality of life is dramatically impacted by policy decisions in Whitehall . Energy costs are more than a third more expensive in the UK than they are in France , and over 70 per cent more than they are in the United States . This is almost all down to the mad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the wider establishment , are prosecuting a war against both hydrocarbons and the laws of thermodynamics . <p> For some years , Britain has been pursuing a net zero agenda that is doing little to actually ameliorate the impact of climate change while increasingly immiserating those of us who live here . We are poorer , colder and less industrious than our peers as a result . Far from leading the way , we are a cautionary tale to the world . <h> Impossible-to-keep commitments <p> There are businesses who have really staked their fortunes on the energy transition , but with waning interest in the States and other nations , this gamble will look foolish . But there are also many companies who , while paying lip service to the net zero agenda , will be quietly longing for a preference cascade that will allow them to be unburdened by these impossible-to-keep commitments . <p> I am not someone who thinks that the climate does n't matter . Far from it -- I think that we have a duty to conserve and even repair the damage done to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ free markets . Instead of the absurd rules around the generation and use of energy , the government should promote supply side reforms that enable providers to flood the system with cheap , plentiful energy . In the short term , that means fracking here in Britain , and switching north sea oil and gas back on . We still need fossil fuels , so we should generate the benefits of doing so here . <p> We also still need hydrocarbons from multiple sources to guard against geopolitical shocks . We were wise not to use Russian energy , a choice that means our economy is n't as hopelessly floundering as , say , Germany 's . But we should be strategic and take energy from all over , spreading the benefits that brings . We could boost our allegiances in the Kurdistan region of Iraq , bolstering the fledgling democracy there . We could encourage Cyprus and the Turkish Republic of North @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a chronic territory dispute along the way ) . The Adam Smith Institute has demonstrated the potential of advanced modular reactors and other nuclear technologies in a recent paper , Fission Impossible . It 's a perfect example of how technological developments will wean us off fossil fuels in a way that does n't crater the economy . <p> So , with the cash we would save by not bankrupting ourselves , Britain could do what it does best -- invent the future . @@121171209 <h> The Debate : Are growth and net zero incompatible ? <p> Are growth and net zero really star-crossed lovers , or can they find a happy marriage ? We get two writers to hash it out in this week 's Debate <h> Yes : Using more to produce less creates a green growth paradox <p> Growth is simple , it 's either inventing new stuff or providing old stuff using fewer inputs . Net zero conversely is a political target that requires the UK to emit zero greenhouse gases ( mostly CO2 ) , on balance , from all economic activity by 2050 . <p> To achieve this first requires the decarbonisation of our energy system , currently 75 per cent dependent on fossil fuels ( mostly oil and gas ) , given energy is the primary input to all other activities . The government 's preferred path is using technologies like renewables ( mainly offshore wind ) that use more inputs ( mostly land and grid infrastructure ) to produce less energy , less reliably , meaning a costly dual energy system to provide back-up . It has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ much longer term . <p> The new stuff then is n't new -- it provides old energy services such as heat , power , and transport in a different way . Nor is it efficient , using more resources to produce less energy means everything costs more , including in renewables supply chains ( for example concrete , cables , and steel ) , creating a ' green growth paradox ' . The best illustration of which is perhaps carbon capture and storage , that renders uncompetitive any process to which it is applied . The things required to achieve net zero make net zero less likely . <p> The solution is technology we do n't yet have , delivered at a pace no one can predict , which is the normal process of innovation , perhaps nudged by a competitive , i.e. low carbon price . Net zero ignores this reality , preferring instead a central planning delusion through five-year targets and climate regulations that obstruct building anything anywhere , while making anything that can be built more expensive , further damaging growth . <p> Net zero will make @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ditch it , leaving markets to drive innovation and change . <p> Andy Mayer is COO at the Institute of Economic Affairs <h> No : Without net zero , climate change will have a disastrous effect on GDP <p> Net zero can -- and must -- go hand in hand with growth . <p> Without net zero , climate change or another fossil fuel price spike will have a disastrous effect on our long-term GDP . And without growth , we will not have the resources to invest in clean technologies . <p> But , to marry net zero with growth in the near term , we need to take a low-cost , market-led approach to reducing emissions that keeps down costs for businesses . <h> Read more <p> Having halved our emissions since 1990 while growing the economy by 80 per cent , the UK has shown that clean growth is possible . Green industries are worth ? 74bn to our economy and grew by nine per cent in 2023 . Commercialising innovative clean technologies offers some of our best prospects both for future growth and limiting global temperature @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of how the UK 's industrial heartlands can be revitalised by a market-led approach to net zero . Thanks to low-tax freeports , investment in sectors such as carbon capture and offshore wind has poured into the former steelworks site in Redcar , bringing opportunity and good jobs back to the area . <p> In fairness they have announced a handful of pro-growth climate policies by reforming environmental regulations and planning rules . But these positive steps risk being betrayed by Labour ministers ' high-tax , high-regulation instincts . <p> Only by removing the barriers to private investment in clean technologies and injecting market forces into the energy transition will we achieve faster economic growth and decarbonisation together . <p> Sam Hall is the director at the Conservative Environment Network <h> The Verdict : A happy marriage requires compromise <p> With Valentine 's Day on the approach , it 's only natural to turn our attention to City AM 's favourite star-crossed lovers : growth and net zero . But are they really destined to destroy one another ? <p> Mr Mayer says a resounding yes , arguing the green @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ use more to produce less ) while climate regulations have made building new projects ( essential to growth ) more expensive and harder to do ( ahem , HS2 's ? 100m bat tunnel ) . <p> But Mr Hall provides a convincing rebuttal , arguing that not only is net zero compatible with growth , it is in fact essential to it . One need n't look far to see that the effects of climate change are expensive . @@121241722 <p> This is Everyday Science with Clare Wilson , a subscriber-only newsletter from The i Paper . If you 'd like to get this direct to your inbox , every single week , you can sign up here . <p> Hello , and welcome back to Everyday Science . <p> This week , I have been thinking about my diet in relation to climate change . We often hear that we should be eating less beef because it is bad for the planet . Yet like most people , I 'm afraid I 'm just not willing to give it up . <p> A perfectly cooked fillet steak is arguably the epitome of good eating . Its humbler cousin , the pack of minced beef , is one of my culinary staples . <p> For a long time I just tried not to think about the fact that my diet is not good for the planet . But lately , I 've been hearing more claims that " regenerative " farming can produce more eco-friendly meat ( and other produce ) . So what does the term mean and just @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ High-fibre diet <p> Cows have such a bad carbon footprint because , along with other ruminants , they have evolved to survive on grass and other leafy plants . Such a diet has very little protein and consists mainly of cellulose , a form of insoluble fibre that is too tough for a typical mammalian gut to digest . <p> Ruminants , though , have a series of four stomachs , which are essentially large bioreactors . These contain bacteria that can break down cellulose and turn it into compounds that mammals can absorb , and ultimately turn it into meat and milk . <p> " In terms of using land for food production that 's not suitable for arable crops , ruminants are able to convert things that we ca n't eat into very nutritious things , " said Professor Chris Reynolds , an agricultural scientist at the University of Reading . <p> The bacteria 's byproduct , though , is methane gas , which cows spend their days contentedly burping , breathing and farting into the atmosphere . That 's a problem , because methane is a potent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heat than carbon dioxide . <p> There are other issues with beef farming , including its high use of energy-intensive artificial fertilisers and diesel-powered tractors . Modern farming has also led to worse soil quality , meaning that the UK 's arable lands now store only half the carbon -- in the form of organic matter -- that they used to , according to the Environment Agency . <p> If that were n't enough , in some countries , acres of carbon-storing trees are being chopped down to make way for large cattle ranches . Together , such issues mean that beef has one of the worst carbon footprints of any food -- as shown in this chart . <h> Regeneration game <p> The answer , some say , may lie in regenerative farming , which broadly speaking involves farms that have both livestock and crops . Such " mixed farms " used to be the norm in the early 20th century , in contrast to most farms today , which generally either grow crops or keep livestock but do n't do both . <p> In mixed farms , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , which avoids the need for artificial fertilisers , and the soil starts storing more carbon . In addition , regenerative farms use more cover crops , to avoid leaving the soil bare , and do less ploughing , both of which seem to promote soil carbon storage and soil health . <p> Conventional farms give cows " cattle cake " , which may be made from soya grown abroad . A key difference on regenerative farms is that cattle are grazed more on pastures , or " grass fed " . <p> The fields are also sown with different plants , mixing clover and wild flowers in with the grass . <p> Some tests suggest such a mixed diet cuts how much methane the cows produce , although it 's not clear why . It might be because such forage has more protein and less cellulose , or that it makes the cows healthier , or that certain compounds in the plants directly interfere with the microbes . <p> Clover also helps improve soil fertility , again cutting the need for artificial fertilisers . <p> For all these reasons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have lower carbon emissions . <p> It can be bought fairly easily online and may also be available from some farm shops . <p> As with most kinds of specialist foods , though , it is more expensive , with a typical pack of mince costing about twice as much as those in supermarket standard ranges . <h> Organic rules <p> While the claims about regeneratively farmed meat are impressive they are not usually accompanied by hard figures about exactly how much carbon is being saved . <p> Part of the issue is that there is no official definition of regenerative farming -- unlike with the " organic " label , which means farmers have to follow strict rules , including on use of chemicals such as herbicides and on space for the animals . <p> Organic farming methods tend to be better than conventional methods for animal welfare , but it 's unclear if organic meat has lower carbon emissions . Some studies suggest it might even have more , because it uses more land . <p> Regenerative proponents say that , because of their use of mixed farms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for the environment than organic farming in terms of biodiversity as well as carbon emissions . " The muck that comes out of a cow , you get worms eating it , you get dung beetles eating it , you get birds reintroduced , " said Alastair Trickett , co-founder of Grassroots Farming , a group of regenerative farms working collectively . <h> Read Next <p> But with no legal definition of regenerative farming , a range of practices at different farms , and little information available on how much each one affects carbon emissions , consumers have to take a lot on trust . <p> We are clearly at a relatively early stage in the regenerative farming movement . But I was cheered to see the Mexican restaurant chain Wahaca saying last week that it had switched to serving regeneratively farmed beef , at no extra cost , and for once , was putting some hard figures to their carbon claims . <p> Wahaca said that its new beef has 42 per cent lower carbon emissions than the average for farms in Europe . That figure was calculated by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , called Farm Carbon Toolkit and My Emissions . <p> It 's good that there is some oversight of companies making green claims , but it does seem like a lot hinges on these organisations getting their sums right . <h> High-tech <p> In future there may be more high-tech ways for beef to become even more eco-friendly . Some scientists are developing food additives , such as from seaweed , which make cows produce less methane . <p> Others are working on making a vaccine that immunises cows against the methane-producing bacteria while another strategy in the works is to try to just breed cows that naturally make less methane . Early research suggests the breeding programme will be possible , although it may be several years before any meat or dairy products from such cattle reach the shelves . <p> Some of these approaches might be a harder sell to the public than regenerative farming , though . In November , there was a social media outcry over Scandinavian Arla Foods ' use of a methane-reducing cattle feed additive called Bovaer in UK farms . <p> The feed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so far is only being used in dairy cattle . <p> Social media posts claimed Bovaer is dangerous . But the Food Standards Agency says the cattle feed additive is completely safe , does n't end up in milk anyway , and is already used in many other countries . <p> Regenerative farming has a more wholesome image . A recent arrival at supermarkets is Regen Milk , from Cornish regenerative farms , although it costs about 50 per cent more than ordinary milk , a similar mark-up to organic . <p> When it comes to meat , if you ca n't afford regeneratively farmed beef , another option may be just to buy British produce , due to its lower carbon emissions , Stuart Roberts of the National Farmers ' Union has said to the BBC . <p> " People say ' cut out meat to save the planet ' , but this message wrongly implies all farms throughout the world have the same carbon footprint , " said Roberts . @@121281061 <h> Christians in a crisis-shaped world : Less a failure than a defeat <p> by <p> 14 February 2025 <p> In an extract from his new book , Jesse Zink argues that Christian formation can be hindered by social structures <p> ISTOCK <p> 0:00 / 0:00 <p> A CLERGY colleague was , at one point in his ministry , responsible for three churches . The third church was the smallest -- just a few people hanging on at Sunday services -- and the parishioners often told him that they felt ignored in the shared ministry . One year , he decided that , to address this , there would be a single service on Good Friday for all three churches , and it would be held in this third church . The congregation of the third church was delighted , and began making preparations . <p> A few days before the service , however , one of the leaders of the third church called . " Well , " he said , " you can still have the service in our church . But none of us are going to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ my colleague with concern . " <p> When my colleague shared this story with me , he said that he felt a tremendous sense of failure . He had ministered among these people for several years , and had done his best to be faithful and to share with them the good news as he understood it . In response , all they could think to do was to go shopping on one of the holiest days of the year ? Surely , he had done something wrong . <p> If you are in Christian ministry today , it can be very easy to feel like a failure . Lots of very well-meaning clergy and lay people are working hard to put together interesting programmes , write compelling sermons , and lead engaging worship . Yet sometimes these efforts just do n't seem to gain traction . People do n't @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ distractedly , or glance at their phones too often . The ministry efforts fail in their intended purpose . <p> Advertisement <p> In recent decades , mainline Christians have struggled mightily to transmit their faith from one generation of believers to the next . It is this , probably more than any other factor , that is the cause of the current fragility of these churches . This struggle has given rise to a narrative among some Christians that suggests there has been a long-formation failure in the Church . <p> The thinking is straightforward . Teaching and instructing people in the Christian faith is vital to forming them as Christians and passing the gospel across generations . If the gospel is not being passed across generations , then Christians must be doing a poor job of formation . If only , this line of thinking goes , we could get our act together and do formation properly , then we could ensure that our Christian communities are thriving . They would come to church on Good Friday instead of heading to the outlet malls . <p> PART of me @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in theological education , and I generally believe that more theological education of all kinds is good for the church . Still , I hesitate . I generally believe that all Christians at all times have sought to be as faithful as they could to the gospel in the best way they could discern . I also know that it is not just mainline churches that struggle to transmit their message . Churches with widely differing formation practices are encountering similar issues . <p> The trouble with thinking that we have individually failed in ministry or that the church has collectively failed is that it places tremendous weight on human action . It is in keeping with the logic of a neoliberal , performance-driven world . But what if it is a matter not of human action but of the structures in which we find ourselves ? <p> That seemed to be the case with my colleague who lost his Good Friday congregation to the outlet mall . His congregants lived within a set of structures that made them desire low-cost goods and made those goods readily accessible through nearby @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ structures in ways that were more powerful than any of his efforts at formation . He had n't failed . He had been defeated . <p> The distinction came to mind when I was a delegate to the 2023 General Synod of the Anglican Church of Canada in Calgary , Alberta . Alberta is the heartland of Canada 's oil production as well as home to much of its agriculture , including cattle ranching , and Calgary is at the centre of both . During the synod , members debated a resolution making worthy commitments regarding climate change , including a commitment by all parishes " to work on reducing greenhouse gas emissions . " <p> It was the kind of resolution that made abundant good sense . By the time of this meeting , much of Canada and the United States had in that summer already endured weeks of intense smoke from wildfires made dramatically worse by climate change . Yet at the same time the resolution felt impotent in the face of the challenge . I was struggling with that sense of impotence when later that same day @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the synod 's closing banquet . <p> As befits Calgary , the banquet was to be a steak dinner held at an event venue called Gasoline Alley Museum . Given the significant carbon emissions associated with eating meat , especially red meat , and the obvious connection between petroleum products and global warming , the synod 's commitments both to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and to eating steak at a museum dedicated to gasoline seemed , at best , incongruous . A friend at synod sent a tart message : " The political economy is stronger than our God . " <p> That moment in synod -- from worthy resolution to emission-producing banquet -- was a moment of defeat for the Church . To say this is simply to recognise that there are powers in this world that are stronger than the efforts of Christians to witness to the gospel , form people in the way of Jesus , and pass our faith from one generation to the next . <p> That we struggle to see this in the Church is an indication of our inability to see with an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clarity , then the nature of the formation defeat -- and the possible path forward -- becomes clearer . <p> IMPLICITLY or explicitly , one way to understand the goal of Christian formation is that it is to help people deepen their commitment to the gospel and the Church . That prompts an important question : Why does a person change religion or make a renewed commitment to it ? <p> For many people , the answer to this question is so obvious it is rarely discussed : a person makes a decision to do so . The Gospels tell us many stories of what seems to be precisely this . Jesus says to James and John to " follow him " -- and they do . What this scholarship suggests is that , contrary to popular belief , religious change is not simply a matter of individual decision . Structural factors matter as well . <p> Understanding the importance of structural factors in religious change does not necessarily contradict how biblical stories of conversion have often been read . The province of Palestine was part of the vast Roman Empire . Economic changes brought about by incorporation into this empire meant that what had previously been an economy based on rural agriculture and small landowners was being transformed into an economy based on large-scale agricultural production for export on huge farms owned by absentee landowners . <p> One result was the creation of a new and growing class of landless poor , who were alienated from the economy as well as from the religious traditions of their time . It is in that outlet mall that we find a clue to the nature of these contemporary structural forces . <p> I THINK the dominant structural forces of a crisis-shaped world are economic . It is hard to proclaim a gospel message that declares our salvation is not dependent on our action , but on God 's , while at the same time living in an environment that incessantly proclaims in implicit and explicit fashion that we are to be judged by our ability , our performance , and our deeds . <p> It is hard to form people into an economy of giving and receiving if the dominant messages we receive are that we are to understand ourselves primarily as consumers who should find meaning through purchase and consumption . His Kingdom had been defeated . <p> But what Jesus on the cross was not , was a failure . He had , in sports parlance , left it all on the field . He had lived confidently , spoken with authority , and confronted the powers directly , and the powers had won . But the great good news of the Christian gospel is found in precisely this : defeat is not the end . Victory is coming . Jesus was defeated , but that does not mean we need to be defeatist . Quite the opposite . <p> Sometimes when I look -- lovingly but honestly -- at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its best to share its message in a crisis-shaped world , it seems like the Church does n't even know what game it is playing , let alone what arena it is taking place in . That path is to see with an apocalyptic clarity that names the powers and principalities that obstruct God 's reign , and then cultivate communities in Christ that share an ethos and set of practices that form people to live in hope , resist the powers of this world , and be a foretaste of the Kingdom that Jesus proclaimed and enacted . <p> Yes , our Christian communities are fragile . Regrettably , cities and local authorities no longer plant arboretums , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from China to Peru . <p> Councils and public authorities are arboreal nativists , polemically committed to planting nothing but " native " trees . Gardeners want flowers and beauty and look for them whether or not they originate in Britain . Along roadsides and batches of new housing , public planters cram in saplings of hawthorn and beech , English oak and those excessive beneficiaries of the nativist agenda , silver birch . Thickly planted , about a foot apart , the majority of these saplings are projected to die long before semi-maturity . <p> In the past , town planners used to plant arboreta of specimen trees from faraway habitats in urban parks and public spaces , ornamenting the landscape and treating the public to beauty and unfamiliarity . An arboretum of recently found trees from China and Chile in modern Hyde Park ? Dream on . <p> In his new book The Tree Hunters , Thomas Pakenham addresses this divergence in the same clear style that made his Meetings With Remarkable Trees a bestseller . He tells many tales of bold collectors before 1920 who went to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ back for cultivation in Britain . He ventures beyond the usual stories of the usual heroes . He then puts the " cult of the arboretum " at the centre of what he rightly calls the transformation of our landscape . I had never joined the two so clearly before . He has form here . Twenty years ago , over-ruling his wife Valerie , he began an arboretum of trees grown from seed he had collected in Tibet and China . It has flourished . <p> What is an arboretum ? A collection of non-native trees , I would say , chosen as specimens for diversity , beauty and unusual features . Pakenham is more strict . He defines it as " a documented collection of trees planted for scientific study or enjoyment " . He wants to distinguish arboreta from woodland gardens , a distinction I would draw by excluding ornamental underplanting and flower beds from a true arboretum . If ageing owners lose the documents that listed their planting , does the result cease to be an arboretum in their heirs ' hands ? Even among the shadows I am sure that Shakespeare never saw an arboretum in a strict sense of the term . Pakenham traces their beginnings back to the 1660s , to the two Tradescants , father and son , and John Evelyn , no one-sided nativist , and to Henry Compton , Bishop of London , perhaps the last such bishop to be an apostle of rare trees and initiator of a truly useful mission , one to bring seeds in from North America . The word " arboretum " had simply meant a " grove of trees " , but by the 1760s it began to be applied to special collections , spearheaded by those in royal ownership that later became the botanic garden at Kew . <p> Compton @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in his case , and " no doubt that of many others " , a collection of trees was " an antidote for disappointment " . He stops his book long before the 1960s , but arboreta have certainly not ceased . Public planters have abandoned them , except in botanic gardens , but private owners have planted superb examples . They include the great collection of oaks at Chevithorne Barton in Devon , assembled by Michael Heathcoat-Amory , and the tree planting in Jonathan Ruffer 's major restoration of Auckland Castle and Bishops Palace in county Durham . Each ranks as a successful investor , never toppled by the market to leave it in disappointment . <p> At Thenford in Northamptonshire , Michael Heseltine , the doyen of Tory ex-statesmen , has spent decades laying out a big arboretum in his massively impressive garden . His arboretum benefited , but it had begun already . <p> Nativist tree planters justly denounce the importing of mature trees from foreign sources and the pests and diseases they may bring in by accident . The foreign trees introduced to British arboreta were mostly grown from collected seed and then propagated for sale quite safely in Britain itself . Nativists also protest that non-native trees do not foster bees , insects or biodiversity . These interrelations are all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ far , than native ones . It is not a native rowan or service tree but a pink-berried Sorbus hupehensis from China . Every year its stale-scented flowers are visited by British insects and then its berries are consumed with glee by British birds in autumn . In my tall Italian alder trees I have thrushes nesting and bees too . Beside them I have been planting yet another winter-flowering cherry , the wonderful Prunus subhirtella autumnalis from China . It remains my top tree for prolonged beauty , never more so than in this wet and grey winter when it began to flower in late November and is still at its finest , with more to come . While many of his policies may , to put it mildly , divide opinion , he certainly ca n't be accused of dithering . If the White House version of a political agent of change resembles a Rambo-esque direct assault on the status quo , Downing Street 's looks more like the chairman of a local ramblers association politely proposing that the group take an alternative , slightly more scenic route to normal . <h> Advertisement <p> Since Labour came to power , it has begun something approaching 400 consultations -- roughly two per working day . On the one hand , this shows that the government has wide-ranging ambitions to make changes , from the seismic to the relatively trivial , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and considered way . On the other hand , while there is likely to be a legal obligation to consult in many cases , it does n't scream agility or urgency , especially when contrasted with the US . Frustration at pressing problems being tackled at pedestrian pace is undoubtedly a contributory factor in Reform 's surge in the popularity polls . <p> The UK has a track record of seeking efficiency through bureaucracy , often in the form of committees , task forces or quangos . I 'm sure the output of many of these will be valuable , but it 's rarely quick . Moreover , these groups are usually spearheaded by veterans and grandees who are , by definition , successful products of the way business was done in the past -- so are unlikely to be sources of fresh thinking . The caricature is of a City fogey spending a year having earnest meetings before drafting a dry , dusty set of recommendations , which the government takes a further year to digest , and where the outcome is another consultation on the measures proposed . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the House of Lords for the author . <p> Elon Musk is definitely a Marmite character . Some of the early moves of his " Department of Government Efficiency " have been criticised as dangerous and will be challenged in court -- but , in theory , I see the attraction of " Doge " as a concept . An independent body , led by a private sector buccaneer , with the executive power to cut red tape and government fat , should be more effective at doing so than the state itself . <p> I suspect the financial markets would react positively to a UK Doge and the notion that government operations might be streamlined by someone with private sector experience . <h> Advertisement <p> The idea is n't entirely radical . @@121301562 <p> Mathias D ? pfner is chairman and CEO of Axel Springer , POLITICO 's parent company . The following excerpt is taken from his new book " Dealings with Dictators . " It was originally published in German by Handelsblatt in 2024 . <p> We are standing on the precipice of a trade war that has Europe in its crosshairs . <p> The World Trade Organization ( WTO ) had barely made it through U.S. President Donald Trump 's first term unscathed . Now , amid a looming wave of " reciprocal " tariffs and threats of retaliation , the world is once again confronted with grave geopolitical uncertainty and a faltering multilateral trading system . So , as we head into this year 's Munich Security Conference , it 's time to reevaluate an institution that is no longer fit for purpose . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Freedom and economic success are closely intertwined . One is usually a precondition of the other . As a general rule , the less free an economic system , the less successful it will be . The one big exception @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ state-controlled turbo-capitalism -- which has , for years , taken advantage of the WTO . <p> Under the cover of " free trade , " China has used its membership to continue expanding its power by unfair means . It turns out that the WTO is n't the solution but a fundamental part of the problem . By accelerating the weakening of truly free economies , it has fostered the rise of unfree and nondemocratic actors . It promotes dependencies and has become a Trojan horse of unfree trade . <p> The WTO was founded in Marrakesh in 1994 . Its establishment led to rules being introduced for services and intellectual property . Previously , international trade rules for goods had been laid down by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade ( GATT ) . The GATT treaty came into being in 1947 with the support of 23 nations . By 1994 , 128 countries had joined . <p> GATT was created following World War II to prevent a replay of the tariff wars of the 1920s . However , what began as a lean and effective collaboration between @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ know today . And it now needs a complete conceptual rethink . <p> WTO members pledge to observe three basic principles when forging international trade relations : trade without discrimination , reciprocity as a basis for negotiation , and the elimination of tariffs and trade barriers . Member states must extend the same advantages to one another . Nondiscrimination further stipulates that the benefits and support granted to one country must automatically be granted to all member states . <p> However , the WTO grants special provisions to countries that define themselves as " developing " -- a classification for which the organization does not provide a formal definition . Members self-declare as " developing , " as China did when joining the trade alliance . The advantages include longer deadlines for implementing commitments or easier market access , among others . But the most important concession is the obligation of other WTO members to safeguard the interests of developing countries when imposing certain national or international measures -- all benefits to which China has been holding on tight since the day of its accession . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ years . The list is long : forced technology transfer ; massive , often undisclosed subsidies ; distortion of competition by state-owned enterprises . <p> In order to gain access to the Chinese market , many foreign companies have had to disclose valuable technological information . The resulting cost to international businesses runs into the billions . Meanwhile , Chinese competitors in some sectors have quickly caught up with industry innovators and become market leaders themselves . <p> Chinese competitors in some sectors have quickly caught up with industry innovators and become market leaders themselves . AFP via Getty Images <p> An almost traumatic example -- especially for Germany -- is that of photovoltaic or solar power systems . Until 2005 , this industry did not exist in China . By 2022 , China 's share in all manufacturing stages had topped 80 percent , based on copied innovation and driven by heavy state subsidies . <p> China views Europe as a self-service shop . With great finesse , it buys into cutting-edge technology , often via " hidden champions " that are less publicly visible than companies such as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and especially its Anti-Monopoly Law -- also have some remarkable features . China likes to penalize foreign companies for being innovative . Anyone who owns a patent and charges licensing royalties for its use can be classified as a monopolist . Smartphone manufacturer Qualcomm was affected among others : It had to pay a fine of almost $1 billion for allegedly demanding excessive royalties from a Chinese competitor . <p> Last but not least , China has n't opened up its markets nearly as much as is often claimed . International companies were unable to fully access its financial sector until 2021 . And a lack of transparent rules means that hardly any business can be done . There have been no successful joint ventures between Chinese and foreign companies in the telecommunications sector . Facebook and Twitter have been banned since 2009 . <p> These examples would be scarcely imaginable the other way around . Chinese companies get to do business largely unhindered in Western markets , while the People 's Republic continues to write its own rules in ways that primarily further its expansion of power . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unable or unwilling to prevent this . Its principle of reciprocity thus remains a pious hope . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> In reality , the WTO is breaking down , tolerating double standards and allowing members to play by different sets of rules . Asymmetry reigns instead of reciprocity . <p> Carbon emissions are another variable that has dramatically grown for China since its accession to the WTO : They 've increased by over 200 percent . And this increase offsets the rest of the world 's decrease by far . China accounted for nearly a third of global carbon emissions in 2021 . That 's more than the United States , India , Russia , Japan and Iran -- the subsequent five largest polluters -- combined . <p> Bottom line , the global climate crisis reinforces the need to take a stand against autocratic systems like China . The real problem with climate change is not the holiday flight to Florida or Mallorca . The problem is that we have little to no influence over the world 's largest carbon polluter . That it pursues a completely different @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that we , ourselves , contribute to it by outsourcing the climate sins we do n't want in our own backyards to China or elsewhere . <p> Viewed from today 's perspective , China 's admission as a full member of the WTO was a fundamental error in a trade policy led by wishful thinking . Motivated , as is so often the case , by good intentions , it created an imbalance that has worsened down the years , much to the detriment of democratic market economies . <p> The main mistake was giving entry to an economically weighty , nondemocratic state , which , due to its own outlook , was unable to adhere to free trade rules . The most ridiculous mistake was to grant China developing country status -- which it still has today despite being the second largest economy in the world -- with all the exceptions and exemptions that come with it . It 's like granting privileges to the most ruthless kid on the block . Competition could n't be more unfair or masochistic . <p> The result of this experiment was predictable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economic success to all participants , but in the long term , it shifted the balance in ways that allowed dependencies and one-sided advantages to emerge . The masochism of the United States and Europe , in particular , led not only to a weakening of their own relative economic power but also , in the end , to an erosion of the entire WTO . <p> And speaking of the end , the WTO has reached the end of the line . What we see before us now is a dysfunctional and paralyzed colossus -- a shadow of its former self . All of which leads to the unsparing conclusion : The WTO should be dissolved . <p> " Dealings with Dictators : A Ceo 's Guide to Defending Democracy " was published by Simon &amp; Schuster in January 2025.

@@121321725 <h> World 's sea-ice falls to record low <p> The world 's frozen oceans , which help to keep the planet cool , currently have less ice than ever previously recorded , satellite data shows . <p> Sea-ice around the north and south poles acts like a giant mirror by reflecting much of the Sun 's energy back into space . <p> But as rising temperatures cause this bright layer to shrink , the dark ocean below can absorb more heat , warming the planet further . <p> This latest sea-ice low appears to have been driven by a combination of warm air , warm seas and winds breaking apart the ice . <p> Over the 5 days to 13 February , the combined extent of Arctic and Antarctic sea-ice was 15.76 million sq km ( 6.08 million sq miles ) , according to BBC analysis of data from the US National Snow and Ice Data Center ( NSIDC ) . <p> This breaks the previous 5-day record low of 15.93 million sq km ( 6.15 million sq miles ) from January-February 2023 . <p> Arctic sea-ice is currently at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ while Antarctic sea-ice is close to a new low in satellite records going back to the late 1970s . <p> The decline of Arctic sea-ice in response to a warming planet is well-established . Its end-of-summer extent fell from an average of 7 million sq km in the 1980s to 4.5 million sq km in the 2010s . <p> But until the mid-2010s , Antarctic sea-ice had been remarkably resilient , defying predictions that it would shrink . <p> Since then , Antarctica has shown a series of very low sea-ice extents , although there is still lots of natural variability . <p> " Every year , every data point that we get suggests that this is n't a temporary shift , but something more permanent , like what we 've seen in the Arctic , " Walter Meier , senior research scientist at NSIDC , told BBC News . <p> " It is indicating that the Antarctic has moved into a new regime of lower ice extents . " <p> Antarctic sea-ice is relatively thin and mobile - being surrounded by ocean rather than continents like the Arctic - @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the ice . <p> But warmer air and warmer waters look to have played a key role in this latest 2025 low , towards the end of the southern hemisphere summer . <p> " Atmospheric conditions in December and January looked like they were strongly promoting surface melting on the ice-shelves , " said Tom Bracegirdle , research scientist at the British Antarctic Survey . <p> " That could also have contributed to what we 've seen in Antarctic sea-ice , and ongoing ocean warming is setting the backdrop to all of this as well . " <p> Antarctica 's record sea-ice low of 2023 would have been a one-in-2,000 year event without climate change , according to a recent study . Yet 2025 is not far from eclipsing it . <p> At the other end of the planet , the Arctic should be reaching its annual maximum , with cold winter temperatures helping the oceans to freeze over . <p> But current sea-ice extent is nearly 0.2 million sq km below anything previously recorded for the time of year , and has been tracking very low since late 2024 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ late freeze-up of ice around Hudson Bay , with unusually warm ocean waters taking a long time to cool down . <p> As well as warmer seas , some storms also disrupted ice around the Barents and Bering Seas , with the consequences likely amplified by long-term reductions in sea-ice thickness . <p> " A thinner ice cover is more responsive to weather ... so weather events can have a stronger impact than they used to , " said Julienne Stroeve , professor of polar observation and modelling at University College London . <p> In recent weeks , Arctic sea-ice has moved even further below average . Temperatures around the north pole were about 20C above normal in early February , leading to melting conditions in places like Svalbard . <p> This " is quite astonishing " for the time of year , according to Dr Bracegirdle . <p> This very low winter extent does n't necessarily mean the Arctic will end up with record conditions throughout 2025 , as conditions can change quickly at the poles . <p> But , with the Arctic warming nearly four times faster than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ almost inevitable . <p> The Arctic is expected to be essentially free of sea-ice at the end of its summer at least once before 2050 , according to the UN 's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change . Some recent studies suggest it could happen sooner . <p> Declining sea-ice at both poles not only has implications for local wildlife like polar bears and penguins , but also the Earth 's climate . <p> " If you significantly change the sea ice distribution in and around Antarctica , you modify that part of the planet which is actually helping us fight against climate change , " said Simon Josey , a professor at the National Oceanography Centre . <p> Sea-ice also plays an important role in the great ocean conveyor , the mass movement of water that helps distribute heat around the planet and keeps places like the UK and north-west Europe relatively mild . <p> " If we see another strong winter loss of Antarctic sea-ice , people are going to start to worry about what it 's doing to the ocean circulation , " said Prof Josey.

However , despite generating over $77 per hour worked , that still sees the UK economy lag behind 13 other European nations . <p> Productivity is said to be the engine of the modern economies -- yet traditional modes of measuring it often fall short , failing to capture the complexity of 21st-century challenges like climate change , biodiversity loss , social transformation , and aging populations . To that end , Strategy&amp; has conceived the new Potential Productivity Index ( PPI ) , to help governments understand where their countries perform well , and where they could help yield greater value . <p> According to Dima Sayess , partner at Strategy&amp; and one of the conceptors of the index , while many productivity models " focus on the past , analysing historic performance rather than identifying future opportunities , " the new model -- developed with the World @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This means it will also examine metrics including human capital , physical capital , social capital , and natural capital -- while factoring in an approach that complements fact-based productivity with ' softer ' measures of advancement . <p> Currently populated with baselines for 60 countries , including the world 's largest economies and a number of emerging markets , the index , will now be used by the firm 's consultants around the globe to provide counsel to government leaders and policy makers . And as that happens , it may well yield important insights for the UK -- where economic growth remains stagnant , something long attributed to struggles with productivity . <p> Showing how the complexity of productivity is often underestimated , official figures in 2023 suggested that UK productivity has barely grown since the financial crisis -- but even so , Strategy&amp; has found the UK outperforms many other global economies . The analysts estimate the UK economy generates $77.40 in value per hour worked , ranking 16th in the world . In particular , it was above the global average when it comes to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> This still ranks the UK behind 13 other European nations , however , suggesting there is plenty of room for improvement . " In the case of the UK , that most overtly seems to be in relation to a long-standing hesitance to address inequality , as well as the investment of its residents in society . <p> When the " distance to best " was measured by Strategy&amp; in these areas , the UK was lightyears away from the study 's leaders . According to the study 's estimations , the country sees an 89% distance to best with regards to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' a rising tide lifts all ships ' , outside of a wealthy minority , many people are simply not benefitting from economic growth . <p> This is leaving a growing number of people feeling they have no investment in the prosperity of the UK . In Britain , social capital -- or the sympathy , and connections created by social interaction within and between social networks -- is at a distance of 95.3% from best in this case . Meanwhile , societal trust , and the idea of being in the same boat , is 95.3% from best . What that might suggest is that if the UK is to kickstart its productivity , tax cuts for billionaires or lumping staff with more responsibilities via AI ' co-pilots ' may not be the way forward . @@121418319 <p> Alternating eerie ambient interludes and bucolic indie-folk pop , the debut from Mirrored Daughters dwells in the spaces between London 's urban sprawl and the ancient trees of Epping Forest . Indeed , the album 's wordless opening and closing tracks are built around the sound of bells and an old violin being physically dragged through the woods , conjuring images of some strange faerie processional happening out of sight on the city 's edgelands . <p> Mirrored Daughters is a supergroup of sorts , a remote recording project by members of London bands The Leaf Library and Firestations , cellist Hannah Reeves , and singer Marlody . There 's an easy kinship between these players -- most of whom have been involved with each other 's projects over the years -- that makes for a warm and welcoming listen despite the record 's occasional moments of unease . <p> ' City Song ' is a soft focus folk song , with Lewis Young 's gentle acoustic guitar consoling a world-weary Marlody as she dreams of escaping an overbearing city to " leave the sound / and your heavy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ upbeat ' The New Design ' , which contrasts typically suburban imagery ( " Still life , the park and ride " ) with a rural landscape where " trees break the pale sky " . Despite this calm , however , the seasons are out of whack and there 's a foreboding to Mirrored Daughters ' Arcadian landscapes . It would be a stretch to call this an album about climate change -- the lyrics are , for the most part , pretty abstract -- but the sense of a troubled environment is present throughout . <p> Elsewhere , ' An Open Door ' has a sundappled ' 60s-ish soft psych lull , reminiscent of Wendy and Bonnie or The Millennium , while ' Unreturning Sun ' hints , perhaps , at an escape from some constricting relationship . ' Something Hollow ' and ' The Lanthorn Daughter ' add pulsing synth lines and recall the calmer moments on The Leaf Library 's dissonant collaboration with Teruyuki Kurihara , Melody Tomb , while the sun-bleached warble of ' Decrowned ' edges towards folktronica . <p> Finally , ' Mirror Ascend ' brings the record full circle . This time , however , the ominous drones have been replaced with a simple guitar melody and distant peals of saxophone . By the end of this evocatively autumnal album , Mirrored Daughters have wandered deep into the forest , but are finally out of the woods .

As far as we know , ours is the only planet capable of supporting life , and it seems to have arisen in the form of something like today 's single-celled prokaryotic organisms . <p> However , scientists have not given up hope of finding what they call LUCA ( Last Universal Common Ancestor , the ancestral cell from which all living things we know are descended ) beyond the confines of our planet . <p> Since humans started dreaming about Martians , scientific understanding has changed significantly . The most recent vehicles to have traversed the Red Planet 's surface -- the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers -- have identified compounds and minerals that suggest its conditions may once have been habitable , but that is the extent of it . <p> Right now , Mars is a reddish desert landscape -- attractive but dead , and certainly not home to any little green men . <p> Other nearby planets offer even less hope . Mercury is a scorched rock too close to the Sun , Venus ' atmosphere is dry and toxic , and the others @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ very far from the Sun . So , apart from Mars , the search for other forms of life is focused on satellites , especially those orbiting Jupiter and Saturn . <p> Europa and Enceladus -- moons of Jupiter and Saturn , respectively -- appear to have large oceans of water under a thick crust of ice that could potentially harbour organic molecules , the building blocks for the origin of life as we know it . These would be nothing like E.T . -- they would look more like the simplest terrestrial single-celled organisms . <p> Looking further afield , more than 5,500 planets have been detected orbiting stars other than the Sun . Only a few are considered potentially habitable and are currently being researched , but as Carl Sagan said in Contact , " the universe is a pretty big place . If it 's just us , seems like an awful waste of space . " <p> Before the 1960s , the conditions on the solar system 's most promising satellites would have seemed impossible for life . <p> The prevailing belief until then was that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ multi-cellular organisms survive . Water , mild temperatures between 0 ? C and 40 ? C , pH in neutral ranges , low salinity , and sunlight or an equivalent energy source were considered essential for life . <p> However , in the mid-20th century , microbiologist Thomas D. Brock discovered bacteria living in the hot springs of Yellowstone National Park , where temperatures exceed 70 ? C. Though unrelated to the search for extraterrestrial life at the time , his discovery broadened its scientific possibilities . <p> Mars is a dead desert landscape <p> Since then , organisms known as extremophiles have been found inhabiting a range of extreme conditions on Earth , from the cold of cracks in polar ice to the high pressures of the deep ocean . Bacteria have been found attached to small suspended particles in clouds , in extremely saline environments such as the Dead Sea , or extremely acidic ones , such as Rio Tinto . Some extremophiles are even resistant to high levels of radiation . <p> What was most surprising , however , was finding them inside ourselves . <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Robin Warren , began studying gastroduodenal ulcers . Until then , the condition had been attributed to stress or excess gastric acid secretion , which did little to help cure the condition . <p> Warren was a pathologist , and having identified bacteria in gastric biopsy samples from patients , he realised that they had to be considered a cause of the disease . However , he had to fight against the dogma that microorganisms could not grow in the highly acidic enivronment of the human stomach . <p> Warren conducted his research alone until 1981 , when he met Barry Marshall , a fellow of the Royal Australasian College of Physicians . He approached Marshall and asked if he would like to work alongside " that crackpot Warren who 's trying to turn gastritis into an infectious disease " . <p> An illustration of a Starship rocket that SpaceX hopes to send to Mars in 2026 ( SpaceX ) <p> In 2005 , Barry Marshall and Robin Warren received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discovery of Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastric diseases , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ H. pylori has an amazing array of factors that help it survive in hostile environments , such as flagella that allow it to surf stomach fluids to get close to the stomach wall , breaking through the protective mucus layer and attaching itself to it . <p> Using the enzyme urease , H. pylori degrades urea in the stomach into ammonia and CO2 , creating a higher pH microclimate that allows it to reproduce . As its numbers increase , it releases exotoxins that inflame and damage gastric tissue in the stomach . This is how ulcers eventually develop , as the underlying connective tissue is exposed to the acidity of the stomach . <p> Their discovery showed that even tucked away in our innards -- in the walls of our stomachs , subjected to vinegar-like pH levels , total darkness , the violent movements of our digestive systems , harmful enzymes and churning tides of food -- life is able to resist and proliferate . <p> The study of extremophile micro-organisms offers the hope that on other bodies in the solar system , or on one of the 5,500 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ phenomenon of life may be present . In 1968 Tennant formed the Mustique Company to further develop the island -- including the creation of the airport . In 1976 Hans Neumann led a consortium that bought a controlling share of the Mustique Company , and in 1987 Tennant sold his remaining shares to Neumann , who in 1988 created the organisation that still exists today -- a private limited company with the homeowners as minority shareholders . Tennant retained a plot on the island until 1992 , when he moved to St Lucia , and bought land there in the hope of creating another Island community . Tennant died in 2010 , leaving his St Lucia home and 95-acre estate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a statue of Tennant on Mustique , recognisable with his cane and his wide-brimmed sun hat . <p> The place remains a home away from home for the royals , although Princess Margaret 's son , David Linley , sold Les Jolies Eaux in 1999 . @@121425860 <h> Accessibility Links <h> Better energy policy could save British industries <h> There is a way to pay for net zero while encouraging the energy-intensive businesses that the UK economy needs <p> Dieter Helm <p> Wednesday February 19 2025 , 9.00pm , The Times <p> It is a sad fact that the UK 's industrial electricity prices are among the highest in developed economies -- higher than in the European Union and about four times that of the United States . The inevitable result is that this country 's energy-intensive industries are uncompetitive . <p> No companies are flocking to the UK to gain access to the promised low energy prices , which were to be the result of switching from fossil fuels to renewables . On the contrary , what is left of UK energy-intensive industries are going for the exit . Grangemouth and Port Talbot are the latest in a long line , including the chemicals industry . The car industry is back to its volume of the 1950s . <p> Not all of this is , of course , the fault of energy prices . Brexit has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Higher labour costs , exacerbated in the autumn budget , and low productivity hardly help , as increases in capital gains taxes add to the competitive disadvantages . <p> All this has one happy consequence for Ed Miliband , secretary of state for energy and climate change : that UK territorial carbon emissions fall as the remaining energy-intensive industries fall , paralleling the falls in the industrial demand for energy . This allows the government to point to the fall in carbon emissions against GDP . <p> Sadly , much of this is smoke and mirrors . By switching from home production to imports , our territorial carbon emissions fall but not , of course , the emissions of the stuff we import instead , and the climate change they cause . <h> Advertisement <p> Part of the problem is that the 60-month sprint to net-zero electricity by 2030 is further increasing the relative cost of UK electricity . Far from being " nine times cheaper than fossil fuels " as Miliband would have us believe , the UK is on the world leaderboard for the highest energy costs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Contrast all this with the US . In Miliband 's world , energy-intensive businesses should be deserting the US in droves to get access to all those cheaper wind farms and solar panels in the UK . The US should be the global loser , and the UK the global winner , as well as the global leader on climate change . In fact , the UK is only a " leader " in mitigating territorial emissions but not in mitigating climate change . It is importing its carbon , and thereby causing higher emissions elsewhere . <p> The truth is that the US is streets ahead when it comes to energy costs -- being the largest producer of oil in the world and having abundant and cheap gas give it a huge competitive advantage . It has so much gas that it was able to bail out Europe when Russian supplies were cut . Contrast that with the UK , which prefers to import its gas in more polluting liquefied natural gas form and by pipeline from Norway , while cutting off its own future sources of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ out of this mess ? What is needed is an international competitive price of energy , and especially of electricity . How might this be achieved ? The same way it was under the " bad old days " of the Central Electricity Generating Board ( CEGB ) . Start with the price that would be competitive . How it was done in the UK ( and in France ) pre-privatisation was to charge industry the long-run marginal costs of energy , rather than the full fixed and sunk costs of the capacity . <h> Advertisement <p> Under the CEGB 's bulk supply tariff , there was an energy price and a capacity cost , to which was added , where appropriate , the transmission and distribution costs . Energy-intensive industry paid the first energy element , covering its variable costs , and it made some contribution to the capacity and network costs . <p> How could this be a sensible economic approach ? Because everyone was better off with these industries rather than without them , as long as they made even a small contribution to the capacity and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ charged the full costs . Imagine that this is uncompetitive and the industries close down . Is everyone better or worse off ? They are worse off , since these industries no longer contribute to the capacity and network costs -- nor , indeed , to the wider economy . To head this off , set a competitive price by charging them the marginal costs and a little of the fixed and sunk costs . <p> This is how it was done from the late 1940s until privatisation . Privatisation eliminated the preferential treatment of energy-intensive industries and accelerated the deindustrialisation that was already under way from the 1980s . The process is exacerbated with the coming of renewables , which are almost all capital costs and have near-zero marginal costs . They are like water pipes and classic utilities . <p> The gap between the marginal and the full costs is ever greater . Under the CEGB approach , the result would have been a great benefit to energy-intensive industries . Under the current approach , there is no preferential treatment for energy-intensive businesses in global competitive markets . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there is a smaller base for recovering all these fixed capital costs . <h> Advertisement <p> If we start instead with the competitive price for large industrial users , then industry costs would fall very sharply . Better still , since the marginal cost of wind and solar is close to zero , it might then actually be true that the UK could be a cost-competitive location . <p> Differentiating the charging between energy-intensive industries and consumers is not straightforward . Why ? Because in a liberalised market , why would a supplier charge less to one class of customer when it can get more money by charging the full price to others ? But it is not as difficult as it seems because the government is now the central buyer for almost all electricity generated . <p> All the renewables and the nuclear are contracted to government , not to customers . Some of the gas is n't , but it is only a matter of time before there will have to be a strategic gas reserve , contracted again through the government . If the government is the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the fixed and sunk costs . De facto , it already is . Hence it can operate a modern form of the bulk supply tariff . <p> Doing what is proposed above is good economics ( it is efficient ) and it is good for the climate . Not doing it means that much of what is left of energy-intensive industries in the UK is effectively finished . Worse , all the ambitions for the UK to become a " world leader " in artificial intelligence , data and quantum computing will be in jeopardy . <p> These new tech industries are the energy-intensive ones of the future . If the government thinks they will all be coming here for the cheap renewable electricity , it can think again if these renewables are priced on a common basis to all customers . <h> Advertisement <p> It is time for the government to get real about making sure that our energy-intensive industries are cost-competitive globally , and real about just how counterproductive for the climate the unnecessarily costly net-zero sprint is becoming . Offshoring emissions is bad for the climate , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Sir Dieter Helm is professor of economic policy at the University of Oxford

They can either form gradually or suddenly appear , ranging in size from a small pit to a massive crater , often swallowing entire buildings or roads -- but what causes them ? <p> ? <h> How do sinkholes form ? <p> According to the British Geological Survey ( BGS ) , " Sinkholes are often saucer-shaped hollows that are the result of some kind of collapse or removal of an underlying layer of rocks that used to support the layer of material at the surface . " <p> Over time , water can dissolve the rock beneath the surface , creating underground cavities . When the ground above these cavities can no longer support its weight , it collapses to form a ' collapse sinkhole ' . <p> " There are several different types of sinkhole caused by different processes , including dissolution , collapse and erosion , " explained the BGS . " Some @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ For example , limestone rocks dissolve when attacked by rainfall or groundwater that is acidic . " Other types of soluble rocks in the UK include gypsum and rock-salt ( halite ) . <p> ? <p> Sinkholes can swallow buildings and roads ( Image : PA ) <p> Some sinkholes are also caused by the erosion of weak , unconsolidated material by flowing water , known as ' erosion sinkholes ' . <h> What triggers sinkholes ? <p> Heavy rain and surface water can cause the ground to collapse over normally stable cavities , forming a sinkhole . As can human triggers such as construction work , which is why sinkholes tend to appear next to buildings and human constructions . But today , it occupies only a fraction of its former range . Typically , breeding colonies reside in cliffs and rocky outcrops , as well as inside castles and ruins in urban areas . The creation of the Souss-Massa national park on the west coast of Morocco in 1991 helped to protect nesting and feeding areas . In 1994 a research program was set up to monitor the endangered species . According to the IUCN , the Moroccan population , which does n't seasonally migrate , is now stable . In 2003 , Fritz , along with his conservation and research group Waldrappteam , began reintroducing captive birds into the wild , but having been raised in zoos they did not know which way to migrate . Inspired by the 1996 film " Fly Away Home , " in which a teenager leads a flock of migrating geese in a hang glider , Fritz concocted the idea of personally teaching the migration path by leading the flock in an ultralight aircraft , flying from Germany to Italy .
